agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 carries both the superscription and the first petition; KJV splits them as 72:0 and 72:1. I translated the whole Hebrew verse. The lamed in lishlomoh is ambiguous (for / of / concerning Solomon); I kept the neutral 'Of Solomon' in the literal layer and noted the options in the commentary.

The jussive reading of the petitions (give / may he judge) follows the imperative 'ten' in verse 1; verbs in vv. 2-17 are imperfects that can be read as wishes or as promises. Four of the five English versions split (KJV/ASV/Webster future, BBE jussive). I chose a wishing voice in the dramatic layer and kept the literal layer tense-neutral ('he judges / will judge').

yashivu (he returns) in the sense 'render, pay back' is why ASV and YLT use 'render/send back'; KJV 'bring' loses the verb. The gloss follows 'they will pay (back)'. Radak and Metzudat David explain it as repeated tribute.

agent_notes: Reviewer request 1: the hitpael 'bless themselves' is now tied to Genesis 22:18 and 26:4 (both hitpael, as here); Genesis 12:3 is cited only as the niphal variant of the same promise. Request 2: the invented quotation is gone from the dramatic layer; the blessing-formula idea stays only in the commentary, attributed to Rashi and Metzudat David, whose wording ('May God make you like Solomon') is a present wish.

yinnon (H5125, from nin 'offspring'): Rashi, Metzudat Zion and one view in Meiri take it as 'rule, lordship' (cf. Prov 29:21 manon); Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Malbim take it from nin 'offspring', a niphal 'be propagated, sprout'. I follow the offspring sense, which the Hebrew 'son/grandson' pair nin and neked supports (Gen 21:23 uses them together), and render 'be continued/sprout' with the 'rule' reading in the commentary. The cross-reference to Ps 74:8 'ninam' is Rashi's, which I could not verify as the same root.

The five English versions split on verb 8: KJV/ASV/Webster 'be blessed in him' (passive, niphal sense), YLT/BBE 'bless themselves' (reflexive). The Hebrew is hitpael, so I choose the reflexive. Likewise the final verb is a piel of 'ashar, 'call happy/fortunate', not a plain 'bless'; KJV 'call him blessed' blurs it with barak.
